title: Understanding Convolutional Neural Networks with scorcher and Internet Cats
text: Breathe in, breathe out. We’re going to embark on a journey to understand a cool R package called scorcher. But before we dive into the code, we’ll start with the very basics of how a computer can “see” and “understand” images, which is the magic behind Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).

title: Understanding Convolutional Neural Networks with scorcher and Internet Cats
section: Part 1: The Building Blocks - Understanding How Computers “See”
text:
Part 1: The Building Blocks - Understanding How Computers “See”
Imagine you’re teaching a child to recognize a cat. You wouldn’t just show them one picture and expect them to get it right every time. You’d show them many different cats: big ones, small ones, fluffy ones, sleeping ones, and so on. In a way, this is how we train a computer.



Different types of cats on the internet


A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is a type of computer program designed to recognize patterns in images. Think of it as a series of filters and transformations that help the computer focus on the important features of an image, just like you might point out a cat’s pointy ears or long whiskers to a child.


What’s in a Picture? Pixels!
To a computer, an image is just a grid of numbers. Each number represents the color of a tiny dot called a pixel. For a simple black and white image, a pixel might be 0 for black, 255 for white, and shades of gray in between. For a color image, each pixel would have three numbers representing the amount of red, green, and blue (RGB).
Our goal is to teach the computer to look at this grid of numbers and say, “That’s a ‘7’!” or “That’s a cat!”.



That’s a cat!





The Core Idea: Convolutions
This is the “C” in CNN and the most important concept to grasp. A convolution is a fancy word for applying a filter to an image. But what is a filter?
Imagine you have a tiny magnifying glass that can only see a small 3x3 square of pixels at a time. This magnifying glass has a special pattern on it. Maybe it’s designed to light up when it sees a vertical edge. This special magnifying glass is our filter (also called a kernel).
Here’s how it works:

Slide: We take our filter and slide it over every single 3x3 patch of our image, from left to right, top to bottom.
Calculate: At each position, we do some simple math. We multiply the numbers in our filter by the pixel values in the image patch underneath it and then add them all up.
Create a Feature Map: The result of this calculation for each position gives us a new grid of numbers. This new grid is called a feature map. This map highlights where the feature our filter was looking for (like a vertical edge) appeared in the original image.




Convolution steps


We can have many different filters, each looking for a different simple feature:

A filter for horizontal edges.
A filter for diagonal edges.
A filter for curves.

By applying several of these filters, we get a stack of feature maps, each one telling us about the presence of a different basic shape in the image.



Making Sense of the Features: ReLU and Pooling
After the convolution, our CNN does a couple more things to process the information.

ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit): This sounds complicated, but it’s super simple. It’s an “activation function” that goes through our feature map and changes all the negative numbers to zero. Think of it as enhancing the important features (the positive numbers) and getting rid of the noise (the negative numbers).




RELU



Pooling: Our feature maps can be quite large. To make them more manageable and to focus on the most important information, we use pooling. The most common type is max pooling. Here’s how it works:

We take a small window (say, 2x2 pixels) of our feature map.
We find the largest number within that window.
We keep only that largest number and discard the rest.
We slide our window across the entire feature map, creating a new, smaller feature map.


This process effectively summarizes the features in a region. It makes our network more robust because even if a feature moves slightly in the image, the pooled feature map will likely still capture its presence.



Putting It All Together: The CNN Architecture
A typical CNN is a sequence of these layers:

Convolution Layer: Applies filters to the input image to create feature maps.
ReLU Layer: Activates the features.
Pooling Layer: Downsamples the feature maps to make them smaller and more focused.

We can stack these sets of layers multiple times. The early layers learn to recognize simple features like edges and corners. The later layers combine these simple features to learn more complex patterns, like eyes, noses, or the shape of a number.
Finally, at the very end of the network, we have a “fully connected layer” that takes the high-level features and makes the final prediction: “This is a cat with 98% confidence.”




Part 2: scorcher - Making CNNs Easy in R
Now that we have a feel for what a CNN is doing under the hood, let’s look at the scorcher package. scorcher is an R package that makes it easier to build and train these complex networks without getting bogged down in the nitty-gritty details. It acts as a friendly interface to a powerful deep learning library called torch.
Let’s break down the MNIST example step-by-step.
# First, you'd need to install the package from GitHub
# install.packages("pak")
# pak::pak("jtleek/scorcher")


The Goal: Classifying Handwritten Digits
The example in the scorcher uses the famous MNIST dataset. This is a collection of 70,000 small, black and white images of handwritten digits (0 through 9). The goal is to build a CNN that can look at one of these images and correctly guess which digit it is.



Step 1: Preparing the Data
library(scorcher)
library(torch)
library(torchvision)

# Training Data
train_data <- mnist_dataset(
  root = tempdir(),
  download = TRUE,
  transform = transform_to_tensor
)

x_train <- torch_tensor(train_data$data, dtype = torch_float()) |> torch_unsqueeze(2)
y_train <- torch_tensor(train_data$targets, dtype = torch_long())

library(torch) and library(torchvision): We load the necessary libraries. torch is the core deep learning engine, and torchvision provides easy access to common datasets like MNIST and tools for working with images.
mnist_dataset(...): This function downloads the MNIST dataset to a temporary directory (tempdir()) if you don’t already have it.
transform = transform_to_tensor: This is a crucial step. It tells R to convert the images from their standard format into tensors. A tensor is the fundamental data structure in torch. Think of it as a multi-dimensional array or matrix that’s optimized for the kind of math we do in deep learning.
x_train and y_train: We separate our data into two parts:

x_train: These are the images themselves (the input). We convert them to torch tensors of floating-point numbers. The torch_unsqueeze(2) part adds an extra dimension to our data, which is needed for the convolutional layers to know that we’re dealing with grayscale images (which have one color channel).
y_train: These are the labels for each image (the correct answers). For each image in x_train, there’s a corresponding number in y_train that tells us what digit it is.





Step 2: Creating a Data Loader
# Create the Dataloader
dl <- scorch_create_dataloader(x_train, y_train, batch_size = 500)

scorch_create_dataloader(...): When we train a neural network, it’s often too slow to show it all 60,000 training images at once. Instead, we show it smaller batches of images. This dataloader is a handy tool that takes our training data and prepares it to be fed to our model in these batches.
batch_size = 500: This tells the dataloader to give our model 500 images at a time. The model will look at these 500 images, make its predictions, see how well it did, and then learn from its mistakes before moving on to the next batch of 500.




Step 3: Defining the Neural Network with scorcher
This is where the magic of scorcher really shines. We define our entire CNN architecture using a clean, readable pipeline.
# Define the Neural Network
scorch_model <- dl |>
  initiate_scorch() |>
  scorch_layer("conv2d", in_channels = 1, out_channels = 32, kernel_size = 3) |>
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("conv2d", in_channels = 32, out_channels = 64, kernel_size = 3) |>
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("max_pool2d", kernel_size = 2)
Let’s break this down layer by layer:

initiate_scorch(): This starts the process of building our model.
scorch_layer("conv2d", ...): This adds our first 2D convolutional layer.

in_channels = 1: This tells the layer that our input images have one color channel (because they are grayscale).
out_channels = 32: This means we want this layer to learn 32 different filters. It will produce 32 feature maps.
kernel_size = 3: This specifies that each filter will be a 3x3 square.

scorch_layer("relu"): This adds the ReLU activation function we talked about earlier.
scorch_layer("conv2d", ...): This is our second convolutional layer.

in_channels = 32: The input to this layer is the output of the previous one, which had 32 channels (our 32 feature maps).
out_channels = 64: This layer will learn even more complex features, creating 64 new feature maps.

scorch_layer("relu"): Another ReLU activation.
scorch_layer("max_pool2d", kernel_size = 2): This adds a max pooling layer with a 2x2 window to downsample our feature maps.

Behind the scenes, scorcher will automatically add the final layers needed to take these feature maps and produce a prediction for our 10 digit classes (0-9).



Step 4: Compiling the Model
# Compile the Neural Network
compiled_scorch_model <- compile_scorch(scorch_model)

$nn_model
An `nn_module` containing 1,199,882 parameters.

── Modules ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• modules: <nn_module_list> #1,199,882 parameters

$dl
This is a dataloader object with features:
 * Batch size: 500
 * Number of batches: 120
 * Dimension of input tensors: 1 28 28
 * Dimension of output tensors: 1

compile_scorch(...): This function takes our model definition and gets it ready for training. It does some important setup work, like figuring out the exact dimensions of the data as it flows through the layers.




Step 5: Training the Model
#-- Training the Neural Network

fitted_scorch_model <- compiled_scorch_model |> 
  fit_scorch(loss = nn_cross_entropy_loss, num_epochs = 10, verbose = T)
  
#> No GPU detected. Using available CPU.
#> 
#> Epoch 1, Loss: 2.02356864586473 
#> Epoch 2, Loss: 0.0940264421204726 
#> Epoch 3, Loss: 0.0601395909674466 
#> Epoch 4, Loss: 0.0492425365373492 
#> Epoch 5, Loss: 0.0394406393170357 
#> Epoch 6, Loss: 0.0305162566791599 
#> Epoch 7, Loss: 0.0269935902828972 
#> Epoch 8, Loss: 0.0224211714424503 
#> Epoch 9, Loss: 0.0192102687200531 
#> Epoch 10, Loss: 0.0172218276983282

fit_scorch(...): This is the command that actually starts the training process.
loss = nn_cross_entropy_loss: A loss function is a way of measuring how wrong our model’s predictions are. nn_cross_entropy_loss is a standard and effective loss function for classification problems like this one. During training, the model will try to adjust its internal parameters (the patterns in its filters) to make the value of this loss function as low as possible.
num_epochs = 10: An epoch is one full pass through the entire training dataset. Here, we’re telling the model to go through all the training images 10 times.
verbose = T: This tells the function to print out progress updates as it trains, so we can see the loss going down with each epoch.

The output you see shows the loss decreasing over the 10 epochs, which means our model is getting better and better at classifying the digits!




Part 3: Alternative Approaches and Deeper Intuition
Let’s play with the scorcher model to build a more intuitive understanding.

What if we use fewer filters?
# A simpler model
simpler_model <- dl |>
  initiate_scorch() |>
  scorch_layer("conv2d", in_channels = 1, out_channels = 8, kernel_size = 3) |> # Only 8 filters
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("max_pool2d", kernel_size = 2)
In this version, the first convolutional layer only learns 8 filters instead of 32. This model would be faster to train but might not be as accurate because it’s not learning as many different features from the images. It has a less nuanced “vocabulary” of shapes to look for.


What if we use larger filters?
# A model with larger filters
larger_filter_model <- dl |>
  initiate_scorch() |>
  scorch_layer("conv2d", in_channels = 1, out_channels = 32, kernel_size = 5) |> # 5x5 filters
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("max_pool2d", kernel_size = 2)
Here, we’re using 5x5 filters. A larger filter can capture more complex patterns in a single step but is also computationally more expensive. The choice of filter size is a trade-off between capturing detail and computational efficiency.
By experimenting with these parameters, you can start to see how different choices in the CNN architecture affect the model’s ability to learn and its final performance. The scorcher package makes this kind of experimentation incredibly straightforward and accessible, even for those who are new to the world of deep learning.

title: PEPCI Project Description
text:
The Pulmonary Embolism Prediction using CXR Imaging (PEPCI) project aims to address the critical need for rapid and reliable tools for diagnosing Pulmonary Embolism (PE), a potentially fatal condition.


Pulmonary Embolism occurs when a blood clot, typically from a deep vein in the leg, travels to the lungs and blocks an artery. While Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the gold standard for diagnosis, it’s not always immediately available or suitable for all patients. Chest X-Rays (CXRs) are far more common, cheaper, and faster to acquire. If AI can accurately identify signs of PE on CXRs, it could significantly expedite triage and treatment.




To collect and curate a diverse, large-scale dataset of CXR images and associated clinical data (including EKG findings) from patients suspected of PE.
To develop and train advanced machine learning models, focusing on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs), for PE prediction using CXR images.
To evaluate the performance of these models comprehensively, assessing accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and other relevant metrics on independent test sets.
To investigate model interpretability (e.g., using saliency maps) to understand the imaging biomarkers identified by the AI.
To explore the potential for multimodal models that integrate CXR data with EKG features and other clinical variables.
To make our research findings, and potentially anonymized datasets or pre-trained models (subject to ethical and privacy considerations), available to the scientific community.
To develop a user-friendly tool (codename: “Scorcher”) for research or educational exploration of PE risk based on CXR features.




This project encompasses data collection, preprocessing, model development, rigorous validation, and dissemination of results. We aim to contribute to both the machine learning and medical imaging fields.



Successful completion of the PEPCI project could lead to: - Faster identification of high-risk PE patients in emergency settings. - Reduced reliance on more invasive or costly diagnostic procedures in certain patient populations. - Improved patient outcomes through timely intervention. - A valuable resource for further research in PE diagnostics.

title: Literature Review
text:
Somani et al. (2022) Paper (Mount Sinai)
Development of a machine learning model using electrocardiogram signals to improve acute PE screening.


The CTPA Overuse Problem

Pulmonary emboli (PE) = blood clots in lung arteries
Potentially life-threatening condition (2-9% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests)
CTPA required for definitive diagnosis but not always immediately available
Only 3-10% of ordered CTPAs are positive for PE
Overuse exposes patients to unnecessary radiation



Study Design

Large-scale retrospective cohort study at Mount Sinai Health System
Novel approach: Combining ECG waveform analysis with clinical data
Study Population & Data

21,183 patients who underwent CTPA evaluation
23,793 CTPAs (10.0% PE-positive)
320,746 ECGs linked to clinical information

title: Literature Review
text:
ML Models

3 Approaches

ECG Model: Convolutional neural network (CNN)

Analyzes raw waveform data from 8 ECG leads
12 residual blocks + fully-connected output layer

EHR data Model: XGBoost algorithm

Uses clinical data (demographics, comorbidities, vitals, labs)
Includes ECG morphology parameters (PR interval, QTc, etc.)

Fusion Model:

Combines ECG waveform embeddings with clinical EHR data
Uses principal component analysis to reduce dimensionality
Built on XGBoost framework




Model Performance

Fusion model significantly outperformed others:

Fusion model: AUC 0.81 ± 0.01
EHR model: AUC 0.65 ± 0.01
ECG model: AUC 0.59 ± 0.01

Fusion model benchmarked against standard scoring systems:

Wells’ Criteria (AUC 0.54); Revised Geneva Score (AUC 0.52)
PERC (AUC 0.50); 4PEPS (AUC 0.58)

Fusion model achieved higher specificity (0.18) vs. clinical scores (0.00-0.05)
Better performance maintained even without D-dimer input

title: Literature Review
text:
Silva et al. (2023) Paper (Portugal)
Artificial intelligence-based diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism: Development of a machine learning model using 12-lead electrocardiogram.


Current Approach Limitations:

Clinical prediction rules + D-dimer tests:

Wells score, Geneva score, YEARS algorithm, PEGeD algorithm

High sensitivity (~90%) but poor specificity (12-30%)
Traditional ECG features unreliable for PE detection
Risk of unnecessary anticoagulation/thrombolysis



Study Design

1,014 ECGs from emergency department patients

All underwent CTPA for suspected PE
911 ECGs for model development (training)
103 ECGs for validation (testing)

Gold standard: CTPA results
Compared AI performance vs. standard clinical prediction rules

title: Literature Review
text:
AI Model and Results


AI Model Architecture

Attention-Enhanced Residual Network
Processes raw 12-lead ECG data (5000 samples/10 seconds)
Pre-processing: low-pass filter + Z-score normalization
Focal loss function to address class imbalance
Self-multi-head attention mechanism for detailed pattern recognition



Key Results

AI-ECG model:

100% specificity (95% CI: 94-100%)
50% sensitivity (95% CI: 33-67%)
AUC: 0.75 (95% CI: 0.66-0.82)

Traditional clinical prediction rules:

~90% sensitivity
12-30% specificity
AUC: 0.51-0.59 (near-random performance)

title: Literature Review
text:
Interesting Finding: ECG vs PE

Traditional ECG features showed no statistical difference between patients with and without PE!

Specific patterns like tachycardia, right bundle branch block, S1Q3T3 pattern, and T-wave inversions appeared similarly in both groups
Even the established Daniels’ ECG score showed no significant difference between PE and non-PE patients

Despite this, the AI model achieved 100% specificity in detecting PE from the same ECG data, which suggests

AI identified subtle, complex patterns that aren’t part of conventional medical knowledge.

Hypothesis: Could augmenting CXR with EKG have merit in predicting PE?

title: Literature Review
text:
Abstract (Houghton et al., 2024, Mayo Clinic)
The AI-Mayo PE (AIM PE) Study: Validation of an Artificial Intelligence Algorithm Using Electrocardiograms to Predict Pulmonary Emboli


Background: The PE Diagnosis Challenge

CTPA required for definitive diagnosis but not always immediately available
Especially challenging in hemodynamically unstable patients



Current Approach: Limitations

Existing algorithms have only moderate accuracy
Guidelines recommend formal scoring systems (Wells’ Score, PERC etc)
Reality: Many clinicians don’t consistently use them
Heavy reliance on “clinical gestalt” (personal judgment)
Risk of missed diagnoses or unnecessary testing

title: Literature Review
text:
AI-ECG


The AI-ECG Approach

Uses routinely collected data (ECGs are standard for cardiac symptoms)
Key Innovation: Combined with D-dimer testing → AUC improved to 0.93



Study Results

Validation using 18,936 emergency department patients
AI-ECG algorithm maintained AUC of 0.69
Three risk categories identified:

Low risk: 0.74% PE rate (99.3% NPV)
Elevated risk: 2.27% PE rate (97.7% NPV)
High risk: 8.02% PE rate (92.0% NPV)

Combined with D-dimer: AUC improved to 0.93

D-dimer is a blood test that detects protein fragments present after a blood clot breaks down.

title: Literature Review
text:
Comparison


Similarities

All utilize ECG data as a core component
All outperform traditional clinical prediction rules
All aim to reduce unnecessary CTPA imaging
All suggest AI can detect ECG patterns invisible to human clinicians



Differences

Data Inputs:

Mayo: Primarily ECG data + D-dimer
Portuguese: ECG data only
Mount Sinai: Most comprehensive (ECGs, demographics, EHR)

Model Architecture:

Portuguese: Attention-enhanced residual network
Mount Sinai: Multiple architectures (CNN, XGBoost)

Performance Focus:

Portuguese: Maximized specificity (100%), Mediocre sensitivity (0.50)
Mount Sinai: Poor specificity (0.18) (although better than clinical scores)

title: Literature Review
text:
Why add CXR?

CXRs widely available and less resource-intensive than CTPA.
Complementary to EKG, routinely performed early in cardiopulmonary workups.
May show secondary PE signs (Westermark sign, Hampton’s hump). (Ask an expert!)
AI/ML models excel at image analysis/pattern recognition.

Challenges

Variable CXR image quality (technique, positioning).
Many other cardiopulmonary conditions could affect CXR appearance and introduce bias.

title: Literature Review
text:
Questions

What variables do we have in addition to the CXR and EKG images?
Do we use the data directly or some engineered version (extract texture features/numeric values)? Or both?
Understanding the timing of when these variables were collected?

What information do we collect for each patient and how and in what stages?
MIMIC data jitters the timestamps.

Why did they do the D-dimer test? Is it not a definitive test? Why not just build a model with EKG+D-Dimer?
Suggestion:

Build models sequentially, first start with EHR, then EKG, then EKG+EHR, then augment CXR and so on.
Understanding variable importance: what variables are important?

title: PEPCEI: Pulmonary Embolism Prediction using CXR and EKG Imaging
text:
Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a life-threatening condition where rapid and accurate diagnosis is paramount. The current diagnostic gold standard, the CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA), while effective, presents significant drawbacks. It imposes a considerable financial burden on the healthcare system and exposes patients to high doses of ionizing radiation, which carries a non-trivial risk of malignancy, a critical concern in a population already battling cancer.



This project aims to address these challenges through a systematic investigation of machine learning (ML) models capable of predicting PE from more readily available and safer data sources. By developing a predictive tool that leverages data from routine Chest X-Rays (CXR) and Electrocardiograms (EKG), we aim to create a powerful, low-cost screening and diagnostic aid. The overarching vision is to enhance early PE detection, thereby reducing morbidity and mortality in our patient populations. A successful model would simultaneously lessen the reliance on expensive CT scans, providing a safer and more efficient diagnostic pathway. This entire study is based on the publicly available MIMIC-IV dataset.



Our technical approach begins with an initial phase focused on pre-computed embeddings to establish a strong performance baseline. For the radiography component, we will utilize the 4,096-dimensional feature vectors from the PhysioNet MIMIC-CXR dataset, which were generated by a state-of-the-art EfficientNet-L2 foundation model. This allows us to leverage deep representations of image abnormalities without the computational overhead of image processing. These rich CXR vectors will be combined with corresponding embeddings derived from EKG waveform data, and the initial models developed to fuse and interpret this data will be based on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures.



Building upon this foundation, the subsequent phase will engage directly with the raw data modalities. A multi-modal CNN architecture will be developed to process both the 2D pixel data from chest X-rays and the 1D time-series signals from electrocardiograms, allowing the model to learn features end-to-end. Looking forward, the project’s ultimate goal is to advance beyond conventional CNNs and explore the capabilities of transformer models.





Develop Novel Models: Creating state-of-the-art CNN and Transformer-based models for PE detection in CXRs.
Curate Datasets: Assembling and meticulously annotating a large-scale CXR and EKG dataset.
Validate Rigorously: Ensuring our models are robust, fair, and generalizable through extensive validation.
Promote Open Science: Sharing our findings, code (where appropriate), and insights with the research community.
Facilitate Clinical Translation: Exploring pathways to integrate our tools into clinical workflows to aid decision-making.






CXR Overview Diagram


Follow our progress through publications, presentations, and updates on this website. We aim to make significant contributions to improving patient outcomes for PE.


Learn more about our Project Description, explore the Data We Use, and see our latest Results.

title: Setup-01: PE Classification with only CXR Embeddings
text:
1. Setup and Libraries
This document details the initial end-to-end process of building, training, and evaluating a deep learning model to predict Pulmonary Embolism (PE) from pre-computed Chest X-Ray (CXR) embeddings. The workflow begins with loading and parsing a complex .tfrecord data format, proceeds through data splitting and pre-processing, defines a sophisticated neural network architecture, trains the model, and concludes with a final, unbiased evaluation.
In the first step, we will set up our R environment. This involves loading all the necessary R packages that provide the functions we need for deep learning, data loading, and general data manipulation.

# Load all necessary packages for deep learning, data loading, and manipulation.
library(torch)         # Core deep learning framework.
library(scorcher)      # High-level wrapper for torch to simplify model building.
library(tensorflow)    # Used specifically for its .tfrecord file reading capabilities.
library(tfdatasets)    # Provides tools to create data pipelines from .tfrecord files.
library(tidyverse)     # Used for data manipulation, specifically the `mutate` pipe.
library(reticulate)    # The bridge between R and Python, necessary for tensorflow.
library(pROC)          # The standard library for calculating AUROC and plotting ROC curves.

# Set seeds for reproducibility of results across runs.
set.seed(612)              # Sets R's random seed for operations like data splitting.
torch_manual_seed(612)     # Sets torch's random seed for model weight initialization.


Code Explanation
The chunk above prepares our session. We load several key libraries:

torch & scorcher: The foundation of our deep learning model.
tensorflow & tfdatasets: A powerful combination used here specifically to solve the complex task of reading the .tfrecord files from the PhysioNet dataset.
reticulate: Allows R to communicate with the Python-based TensorFlow library.
tidyverse: We use it here for clean data manipulation functions and later for ggplot2.

title: Setup-01: PE Classification with only CXR Embeddings
text:
2. Metadata Loading and Cleaning
Here, we will load the CXRembeddingfile.csv. This file acts as our map, linking the path of each embedding file to its corresponding clinical label (PE positive or negative). We will also perform a cleaning step to make the file paths portable.

Load the CSV file into an R data frame.
Inspect the file paths, which are specific to the original user’s machine.
Remove the user-specific prefix from the file paths to make them relative and portable.
Verify that the labels in the file are valid (i.e., only 0s and 1s).


# Define the path to the CSV file that maps embeddings to labels.
metadata_file <- "CXR/CXRembeddingfile.csv"

# Read the metadata and make file paths portable.
embedding_metadata <- read.csv(metadata_file) |>
  # Remove original specific filepaths
  mutate(filepath = str_replace(filepath, "^/Users/[^/]+/Desktop/", "")) |>
  # Ensure we only have the columns we need.
  dplyr::select(filepath, label)

# This is a defensive check to ensure our label data is clean.
if (!all(embedding_metadata$label %in% c(0, 1))) {
  stop("Invalid labels found. Expected only 0 and 1.")
}

cat("Successfully loaded and cleaned metadata for", nrow(embedding_metadata), "CXR records.")

Successfully loaded and cleaned metadata for 3590 CXR records.

title: Setup-01: PE Classification with only CXR Embeddings
text:
3. TFRecord Parsing and Data Loading
We now need to read the actual embedding vectors, which are stored in a special binary format called .tfrecord.

Define a special “parser” function that teaches R and TensorFlow how to interpret the structure of our specific .tfrecord files.
Create a tfdatasets pipeline that applies this parser to every file path from our metadata.
Execute the pipeline, iterating through every file and converting the TensorFlow tensors into R-native objects.
Combine the list of vectors into a single large matrix.
Adjust the labels for R’s indexing system (from 0-1 to 1-2).


# Define a function to parse a single .tfrecord file.
parse_embedding_fn <- function(proto) {
  # Describe the structure of the data inside the .tfrecord file.
  features <- list(
    # The feature 'embedding' is stored as a variable-length list of floats.
    embedding = tensorflow::tf$io$VarLenFeature(dtype = tensorflow::tf$float32)
  )
  # Parse the binary record using the defined structure.
  parsed_features <- tensorflow::tf$io$parse_single_example(proto, features)
  # VarLenFeature creates a SparseTensor; convert it to a normal (dense) tensor.
  embedding_vector <- tensorflow::tf$sparse$to_dense(parsed_features$embedding)
  # Ensure the output is a flat 1D vector.
  tensorflow::tf$reshape(embedding_vector, shape = list(-1L))
}

# Create a dataset pipeline object from the filepaths.
tf_dataset <- tfrecord_dataset(embedding_metadata$filepath) |>
  # Apply our parsing function to each file in the dataset.
  dataset_map(parse_embedding_fn)

# Execute the pipeline and load all embeddings into R.
# reticulate::iterate calls the tensor's .numpy() method to convert it to an R object.
embedding_list <- reticulate::iterate(tf_dataset, f = function(x) x$numpy())
# Combine the list of individual embedding vectors into a single matrix.
all_embeddings <- do.call(rbind, embedding_list)

# Get the labels vector and add 1 to convert from 0/1 to 1/2.
# This is required for R's 1-based indexing in the torch loss function.
outcome_labels <- embedding_metadata$label + 1

cat("--- Data Loading Complete ---\n")

--- Data Loading Complete ---

cat("Loaded", nrow(all_embeddings), "embeddings with", ncol(all_embeddings), "features each.\n\n")

Loaded 3590 embeddings with 1376 features each.



Code Explanation
This chunk is the result of our extensive debugging and represents the correct way to load this specific dataset.

parse_embedding_fn: This function is the instruction manual for reading a single file. We discovered through debugging that the data is stored as a VarLenFeature (variable-length feature). Inside the function, we parse the file, convert the data from its special “sparse” format to a regular “dense” vector, and reshape it to ensure it’s a flat list of numbers.
tfrecord_dataset(): This creates the initial dataset object, which is essentially a list of file paths.
dataset_map(): This applies our parser function across the entire dataset.
reticulate::iterate(): This is the key function that executes the pipeline. It loops through every parsed record and uses the .numpy() method to convert the TensorFlow tensor into an R-friendly format.
do.call(rbind, ...): This is an efficient R function for taking a list of vectors and stacking them together row-by-row to create our final all_embeddings matrix.
+ 1: We add 1 to the labels (0, 1) to turn them into (1, 2). This is critical because torch in R expects class indices to start at 1, not 0.

title: Setup-01: PE Classification with only CXR Embeddings
text:
4. Data Splitting
To build a reliable model, we must separate our data into distinct sets.

Training Set (70%): The data the model learns from.
Testing Set (15%): Data used during training to monitor for overfitting.
Validation Set (15%): The “lockbox” data, used only once at the very end for a final, unbiased performance evaluation.


cat("--- Splitting Data ---\n")

--- Splitting Data ---

num_samples <- nrow(all_embeddings)
# Shuffle indices to ensure random distribution of data across splits.
shuffled_indices <- sample(num_samples)

# Define the size of each dataset split.
train_size <- floor(0.70 * num_samples)
test_size <- floor(0.15 * num_samples)

# Get the indices for each set from the shuffled list.
train_indices <- shuffled_indices[1:train_size]
test_indices <- shuffled_indices[(train_size + 1):(train_size + test_size)]
val_indices <- shuffled_indices[(train_size + test_size + 1):num_samples]

# Subset the embeddings and labels into their respective sets using the indices.
x_train <- all_embeddings[train_indices, ]
y_train <- outcome_labels[train_indices]

x_test <- all_embeddings[test_indices, ]
y_test <- outcome_labels[test_indices]

x_val <- all_embeddings[val_indices, ]
y_val <- outcome_labels[val_indices]

cat("Training samples:", nrow(x_train), "\n")

Training samples: 2513 

cat("Testing samples (for epoch monitoring):", nrow(x_test), "\n")

Testing samples (for epoch monitoring): 538 

cat("Validation samples (final lockbox):", nrow(x_val), "\n\n")

Validation samples (final lockbox): 539

title: Setup-01: PE Classification with only CXR Embeddings
text:
5. Tensor Conversion & DataLoader
The torch library has its own highly optimized data format called a “tensor.” We must convert all our data into this format. We also create a DataLoader using the scorch package, which is a tool that feeds data to the model in small, efficient batches during training.

# Convert all R matrices and vectors into torch tensors.
x_train <- torch_tensor(x_train)
y_train <- torch_tensor(y_train, dtype = torch_long())
x_test <- torch_tensor(x_test)
y_test <- torch_tensor(y_test, dtype = torch_long())
x_val <- torch_tensor(x_val)
y_val <- torch_tensor(y_val, dtype = torch_long())

# Create a dataloader to feed the training data to the model in batches.
dl <- scorch_create_dataloader(x_train, y_train, batch_size = 32)
# Dynamically get the embedding dimension from the data.
embedding_dim <- ncol(x_train)


Code Explanation

torch_tensor(): The primary function for converting R objects to torch tensors. The dtype = torch_long() is important for the labels, as classification loss functions expect integer-type labels.
scorch_create_dataloader(): This scorcher function simplifies the creation of a dataloader. A batch_size = 32 means the model will look at 32 samples at a time before updating its weights.

title: Setup-01: PE Classification with only CXR Embeddings
text:
6. Model Architecture Definition
Now we define the “brain” of our operation—the neural network itself. This is a moderately complex architecture designed to be powerful enough for this task. It is organized into logical blocks and uses Batch Normalization and Dropout.

cat("\n--- Building Balanced Model Architecture ---\n")


--- Building Balanced Model Architecture ---

# Define a moderately complex neural network architecture using a scorcher pipeline.
scorch_model <- dl |>
  initiate_scorch() |>
  # === INPUT PROCESSING ===
  # Expands features and applies immediate regularization.
  scorch_layer("linear", in_features = embedding_dim, out_features = 512) |>
  scorch_layer("batch_norm1d", num_features = 512) |>
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("dropout", p = 0.2) |>
  
  # === FEATURE EXTRACTION BLOCK 1 ===
  # Uses a sigmoid 'gate' to help the model select important features.
  scorch_layer("linear", in_features = 512, out_features = 384) |>
  scorch_layer("batch_norm1d", num_features = 384) |>
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("linear", in_features = 384, out_features = 384) |>
  scorch_layer("sigmoid") |>
  scorch_layer("dropout", p = 0.3) |>
  
  # === FEATURE EXTRACTION BLOCK 2 ===
  # Uses tanh activation to bound features between -1 and 1.
  scorch_layer("linear", in_features = 384, out_features = 256) |>
  scorch_layer("batch_norm1d", num_features = 256) |>
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("linear", in_features = 256, out_features = 256) |>
  scorch_layer("batch_norm1d", num_features = 256) |>
  scorch_layer("tanh") |>
  scorch_layer("dropout", p = 0.4) |>
  
  # === CLASSIFICATION HEAD ===
  # Reduces features down to the final class outputs.
  scorch_layer("linear", in_features = 256, out_features = 128) |>
  scorch_layer("batch_norm1d", num_features = 128) |>
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("linear", in_features = 128, out_features = 64) |>
  scorch_layer("batch_norm1d", num_features = 64) |>
  scorch_layer("relu") |>
  scorch_layer("dropout", p = 0.3) |>
  
  # Final Output Layer: Produces raw scores (logits) for our 2 classes.
  scorch_layer("linear", in_features = 64, out_features = 2)

# Compile the defined architecture into a trainable torch model.
compiled_scorch_model <- compile_scorch(scorch_model)
compiled_scorch_model

$nn_model
An `nn_module` containing 1,258,690 parameters.

── Modules ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• modules: <nn_module_list> #1,258,690 parameters

$dl
This is a dataloader object with features:
 * Batch size: 32
 * Number of batches: 79
 * Dimension of input tensors: 1376
 * Dimension of output tensors: 1



Code Explanation
This scorcher pipeline defines a deep neural network layer-by-layer.

scorch_layer("linear", ...): A standard fully-connected layer. in_features must match the output of the previous layer, and out_features defines the size of the next layer.
scorch_layer("relu"): The main activation function, allowing the model to learn non-linear patterns.
scorch_layer("batch_norm1d", ...): Normalizes the outputs of the previous layer, which helps stabilize and speed up training.
scorch_layer("dropout", p = ...): A regularization technique that randomly sets a proportion (p) of neuron activations to zero during training to prevent overfitting.
compile_scorch(): This finalizes the model definition and prepares it for training.

Of course. Here is a summary of the model architecture from the final script, incorporating the explanations for why each layer and its specific values were chosen.



Summary of the Model Architecture
The model is a deep, feed-forward neural network designed to classify Pulmonary Embolism (PE) risk from high-dimensional (4096) CXR embedding vectors. The architecture follows a sophisticated “funnel” design, progressively reducing the dimensionality of the features while using a combination of modern techniques to stabilize training and prevent overfitting. It is organized into distinct logical blocks:

1. Input Processing Block (4096 → 512 features)
This initial block serves to compress the large, sparse input embedding into a more manageable and dense feature representation.

linear(4096, 512): The first layer performs a crucial transformation, reducing the feature dimension from 4096 to 512. This forces the model to create a dense summary of the initial information.
batch_norm1d: Immediately follows the linear layer to stabilize its output, which is critical when dealing with such a large input dimension.
relu: The standard activation function introduces non-linearity, allowing the model to learn complex patterns.
dropout(p=0.2): A light dropout is applied. This provides initial regularization without discarding too much potentially valuable information from the input embedding.



2. Feature Extraction Block 1 (512 → 384 features)
This block continues to refine features and introduces a “gating” mechanism to help the model learn which features are most important.

linear & relu: The network continues to process and transform the 512 features into a 384-feature space.
sigmoid Gate: A unique feature of this block is a linear layer followed by a sigmoid activation. This sigmoid function squashes its output to a range between 0 and 1, effectively acting as a learned “gate” that can scale down the importance of less relevant features before passing them to the next stage.
dropout(p=0.3): A slightly higher dropout rate is applied after the gating mechanism for regularization.



3. Feature Extraction Block 2 (384 → 256 features)
This block further distills the features and introduces a “bounding” mechanism.

linear & relu: The feature space is further reduced from 384 to 256 dimensions.
tanh Activation: This activation function bounds the feature values to a range between -1 and 1. This “centering” of the data can help stabilize learning in the subsequent layers.
dropout(p=0.4): The dropout rate is increased again. As the features become more abstract and complex, we can apply stronger regularization to ensure the model is learning generalizable patterns.



4. Classification Head (256 → 64 features)
This is the final stage of feature processing, where the network funnels the highly abstract features into a compact representation just before the final decision.

Two linear + relu Blocks: The feature space is decisively reduced from 256 to 128, and then to a final, compact set of 64 features.
dropout(p=0.3): One last application of dropout provides final regularization before the output layer.



5. Output Layer (64 → 2 features)
This is the final decision-making layer of the model.

linear(64, 2): This layer takes the final 64-feature vector and produces exactly two raw numbers (logits). Each number represents the model’s calculated score for one of the two classes (Class 1: No PE, Class 2: PE). These scores are then fed into the loss function during training and the argmax function during evaluation.

title: Setup-01: PE Classification with only CXR Embeddings
text:
7. Model Training
This is where the learning occurs. We will feed the training data to our compiled model for a set number of “epochs” (passes through the data). After each epoch, we will check the model’s performance on our “test” set to monitor its progress.

cat("\n--- Starting Model Training ---\n")


--- Starting Model Training ---

# Train the model using the training data.
fitted_scorch_model <- compiled_scorch_model |>
  fit_scorch(
    loss = nn_cross_entropy_loss,      # Standard loss function for multi-class classification.
    num_epochs = 25,                   # Number of passes through the entire training data.
    verbose = TRUE,                    # Print progress during training.
    validation_data = list(x_test, y_test) # Monitor performance on the test set after each epoch.
  )

title: Setup-01: PE Classification with only CXR Embeddings
text:
8. Final Evaluation
This is the final step. We take the fully trained model and evaluate its performance on the “validation” data that it has never seen before. This provides an unbiased assessment of our model’s predictive power.

cat("\n--- FINAL PERFORMANCE ON VALIDATION SET ---\n")


--- FINAL PERFORMANCE ON VALIDATION SET ---

# Set model to evaluation mode and disable gradient calculation for efficiency.
with_no_grad({
  # Get model predictions by calling the fitted model object directly on the validation data.
  predictions <- fitted_scorch_model(x_val)
})

# Convert model outputs (logits) to predicted class labels.
# --- Convert Model Output to Class Predictions ---
predicted_classes <- as_array(torch_argmax(predictions, dim = 2)) 

# Get the actual labels (which are 1 and 2) for comparison.
actual_classes <- as_array(y_val)

# --- Calculate Metrics from the Confusion Matrix ---
cat("\n--- Confusion Matrix ---\n")


--- Confusion Matrix ---

confusion_matrix <- table(Predicted = predicted_classes, Actual = actual_classes)
print(confusion_matrix)

         Actual
Predicted   1   2
        1 451  41
        2  37  10

# Extract the four components of the confusion matrix.
# We assume that Class '2' (original label '1') is the "positive" class.
TP <- confusion_matrix[2, 2] # True Positives
TN <- confusion_matrix[1, 1] # True Negatives
FP <- confusion_matrix[2, 1] # False Positives
FN <- confusion_matrix[1, 2] # False Negatives

# Calculate overall accuracy.
accuracy <- sum(diag(confusion_matrix)) / sum(confusion_matrix)
# Calculate Sensitivity (Recall).
sensitivity <- TP / (TP + FN)
# Calculate Specificity.
specificity <- TN / (TN + FP)
